explanation:
### Reporting in time order

```cpp
std::vector<Event> held;
held.reserve(buf.size());
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < buf.size(); ++i) held.push_back(buf.at(i));
std::stable_sort(held.begin(), held.end(),
                 [](const Event& a, const Event& b) { return a.at < b.at; });
```

Three decisions in four lines.

**A copy, not the buffer.** `report` must leave the buffer as it found it —
there is a case that reports, dumps and reports again. Sorting through the
public interface is not possible anyway, which is the interface doing its job.

**`stable_sort`, not `sort`.** Two events stamped at the same millisecond have
to come out in the order they arrived. `std::sort` is allowed to reorder
elements it considers equal, and in practice it does; `std::stable_sort`
promises it will not. This is the one line of this milestone that a sample
case cannot catch and a hidden case can.

**`a.at < b.at`, and nothing else.** A comparator that also compares the text
breaks ties by spelling, which is not what was asked. A comparator using `<=`
is worse: it is not a strict weak ordering, and the standard library is
allowed to do anything at all with one — including run off the end of the
array. It is undefined behaviour that usually looks like it works.

### Why arrival order and event order differ

They are different clocks. Events arrive when the network, the scheduler and
the buffering decide; they *happened* when the thing that logged them says
they did. Any system that collects from more than one source has to deal with
out-of-order arrival, and the usual answer is exactly this: keep a window,
and sort it on the way out.

### The whole project

Three milestones, one codebase: a bounded structure, then a policy for what
to do when it is full, then a view over what it holds. The second and third
are the ones that would be awkward to bolt on later, and both were cheap here
because the first one kept its state in one place.
